title: SQL vs NoSQL
objectives: Explain SQL vs NoSQL with measurable requirements and failure modes
Apply SQL vs NoSQL to a high-traffic India-scale scenario in an interview

cards.title: text
cards.body: Interview lens on SQL vs NoSQL: open with actors, peak traffic shape, and explicit non-goals so the conversation stays bounded like a production RFC review (topic 21).

cards.title: text
cards.body: Mental model for SQL vs NoSQL: map each user action to a synchronous vs asynchronous hop, then mark which hops need strong invariants versus where stale reads are tolerable.

cards.title: diagram
cards.body: Walk a hot read path for SQL vs NoSQL: client → DNS/TLS → edge → service → cache → store. Call out where you would measure p95 and which hop fails first under 10× diurnal peak.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Failure mode in SQL vs NoSQL: retries without idempotency, cache stampedes, or unbounded fan-out often hurt before raw CPU; name the guardrail you add first for this topic.

cards.title: animation
cards.body: Say aloud for SQL vs NoSQL: (1) user story in one sentence, (2) two numbers (QPS + data size), (3) one trade-off you will revisit in the deep dive.

questions.prompt: For SQL vs NoSQL, which first step best reduces ambiguity in a system design interview?

choices.label: List user actions, scale, and latency/durability targets

questions.explanation: Strong interviews anchor on requirements and SLOs before components.

questions.prompt: Where is the first saturation point in a naive single-region SQL vs NoSQL design under flash traffic?
questions.explanation: Unsharded OLTP primaries usually exhaust connections/IOPS before stateless tiers.

questions.prompt: Order a crisp interview flow when presenting SQL vs NoSQL.

items.label: Deep dive hot path and failures

questions.explanation: Numbers before boxes keeps trade-offs honest.

questions.prompt: SQL vs NoSQL: 2.4M read requests/day spread uniformly. Estimate average read QPS (nearest integer).
questions.workedAnswer: 2.4M/day ≈ 27.8 QPS average; plan higher for peak factors.
questions.explanation: Convert daily volume to per-second capacity before sizing caches and DB pools.

questions.prompt: Choose an approach to handle 5× lunch-hour spikes for SQL vs NoSQL.

rationaleOptions.label: Stateless tiers absorb burst without one machine ceiling
Caching shifts read load off the primary
Vertical scale cannot survive AZ loss by itself

questions.explanation: Horizontal stateless scaling plus caching is the common interview answer for read-heavy bursts.

questions.prompt: Which NON-functional requirement is most central to SQL vs NoSQL?

choices.label: Correctness under retries and partial failures

questions.explanation: Distributed systems fail partially; interviews probe how you preserve invariants.

flashcards.front: What is the core interview takeaway for SQL vs NoSQL?
flashcards.back: Connect user journeys to SLOs, then justify components and trade-offs for SQL vs NoSQL.

flashcards.front: Name one pitfall when discussing SQL vs NoSQL.
flashcards.back: Skipping scale numbers, ignoring retries/idempotency, or mixing AuthN with AuthZ.

flashcards.front: Which metric would you cite first for SQL vs NoSQL?
flashcards.back: p95 latency on the hot path plus error rate on writes/reads that affect revenue or safety.

questions.prompt: A bank transfer touches 2 rows. How many row locks minimum in two-phase locking for serializability?

RC allows concurrent bookings to pass checks

questions.explanation: Inventory systems need repeatable reads or serializable semantics on hot rows.

questions.explanation: Phantoms need predicate locking or serializable isolation.

R=1 breaks strong read guarantee

questions.explanation: When staleness is unacceptable, keep R and W high enough for overlap.

questions.prompt: Sloppy quorums are used to:

title: CAP
objectives: Explain CAP with measurable requirements and failure modes
Apply CAP to a high-traffic India-scale scenario in an interview

cards.title: CAP in one minute
cards.body: In distributed systems, Partition tolerance is mandatory on WANs. During a network split, you must trade Availability vs Consistency (CP vs AP).

cards.title: Not a menu of three
cards.body: CAP is about behavior during partitions, not steady state. Normal operation still has latency/consistency trade-offs (see PACELC).

cards.title: Split brain sketch
cards.body: Draw two islands of replicas that cannot talk; decide whether each island keeps serving writes (AP) or stops (CP).
cards.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#22d3ee'/><text x='40' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Client</text><rect x='90' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#a78bfa'/><text x='120' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Edge</text><rect x='170' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#34d399'/><text x='200' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Svc</text><rect x='250' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#f472b6'/><text x='280' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Data</text><line x1='70' y1='60' x2='90' y2='60' stroke='#94a3b8'/><line x1='150' y1='60' x2='170' y2='60' stroke='#94a3b8'/><line x1='230' y1='60' x2='250' y2='60' stroke='#94a3b8'/></svg>

cards.title: Product mapping
cards.body: Bank balances lean CP; social feeds lean AP with repair. Call out which user-visible symptom is acceptable during a blip.

cards.title: Say aloud
cards.body: Script: define C/A/P → admit partitions happen → pick CP or AP for the split → give an example.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, what must a CP system sacrifice according to the CAP theorem framing used in interviews?
questions.explanation: Under partition, CP systems refuse or delay responses to preserve consistency.

questions.prompt: Which component is the usual bottleneck when AP caches serve stale reads during a partition?
questions.explanation: Repair pipelines and conflict resolution lag when replicas diverge.

questions.prompt: Order the CAP interview explanation.

items.label: Define C, A, P in distributed context
State that partitions happen in real networks
Explain CP vs AP choice during partition
Give a product example (bank ledger vs social feed)

questions.explanation: Interviewers want precise definitions before examples.

questions.prompt: A service must remain available during a partition and accepts stale reads. If 40% of replicas are isolated, what fraction of users might see stale data at worst (assume uniform routing)?
assumptions: Isolated replicas cannot receive latest writes
questions.workedAnswer: Up to ~40% of traffic routed to isolated replicas may read stale values until repair.
questions.explanation: AP systems expose inconsistency windows tied to replica isolation.

questions.prompt: Pick a datastore posture for a social 'like' counter during partitions.

approaches.label: CP SQL with global serializability
approaches.description: May reject writes when minority partition

rationaleOptions.label: Likes are soft state; convergence beats global locks
Availability matches user expectation during network blips
Global serializability is costly for high fan-out writes

questions.explanation: AP fits high-churn soft state; repair merges counts later.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CAP is interview-correct?

choices.label: You can pick all three always
Partition tolerance is mandatory in WAN systems; choose C vs A during partition
CAP only applies to SQL databases

questions.explanation: Real networks partition; design chooses consistency vs availability for that window.

flashcards.back: Skipping scale numbers, ignoring retries/idempotency, or mixing AuthN with AuthZ.

flashcards.front: Which metric would you cite first for CAP?
flashcards.back: p95 latency on the hot path plus error rate on writes/reads that affect revenue or safety.

title: PACELC
objectives: Explain PACELC with measurable requirements and failure modes
Apply PACELC to a high-traffic India-scale scenario in an interview

cards.title: PACELC expands CAP
cards.body: If Partition: choose Availability vs Consistency. Else (normal network): choose Latency vs Consistency (EL vs EC).

cards.title: Label systems
cards.body: Dynamo/Cassandra are often PA/EL; Spanner-like systems target PC/EC with higher latency budgets.

cards.title: Replica read paths
cards.body: Show leader writes plus follower reads that may lag; tie lag to business staleness budgets.
cards.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#22d3ee'/><text x='40' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Client</text><rect x='90' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#a78bfa'/><text x='120' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Edge</text><rect x='170' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#34d399'/><text x='200' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Svc</text><rect x='250' y='40' width='60' height='40' fill='#1e293b' stroke='#f472b6'/><text x='280' y='65' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>Data</text><line x1='70' y1='60' x2='90' y2='60' stroke='#94a3b8'/><line x1='150' y1='60' x2='170' y2='60' stroke='#94a3b8'/><line x1='230' y1='60' x2='250' y2='60' stroke='#94a3b8'/></svg>

cards.title: Latency math
cards.body: Cross-region strong reads add RTT; EL reads from local replicas shave milliseconds but allow temporary divergence.

cards.title: Say aloud
cards.body: Explain CAP for partitions, then PACELC for steady state with a catalog pricing example.

questions.prompt: PACELC adds which trade-off when the network is normal (E/L)?

choices.label: Batch vs stream only for ETL

questions.explanation: Else (normal operation), choose latency vs consistency (PACELC).

questions.prompt: In a PA/EL system, which layer usually hides replication lag first?
questions.explanation: Reading from async followers trades consistency for latency.

questions.prompt: Order PACELC explanation steps.
questions.explanation: PACELC bridges partition behavior and steady-state latency.

questions.prompt: If a quorum read requires contacting 2 of 3 replicas with 8ms RTT each (parallel), what is approximate read latency?
assumptions: Dominant term is max RTT among quorum
questions.workedAnswer: Parallel quorum read ≈ 8ms if one replica suffices in same AZ.
questions.explanation: Latency math supports EL choices.

questions.prompt: Choose read strategy for a product catalog during normal operation.

approaches.label: Read from async replicas with TTL

rationaleOptions.label: Catalog is EL-friendly; staleness bounded by TTL
Avoids cross-region leader reads on every request
Linearizable global reads violate latency goal

questions.explanation: PA/EL pattern: accept eventual consistency for latency when business allows.

questions.prompt: Dynamo-style systems are often labeled:
questions.explanation: Dynamo prioritizes availability/partition tolerance and low latency with eventual consistency.
